Let \(P\) have integer coefficients. For integers \(m,n\), \(m-n\mid P(m)-P(n)\).

From \(P(1)=a\) and \(P(4)=-a\), we get \(3\mid 2a\), so \(3\mid a\).  
From \(P(1)=a\) and \(P(6)=-a\), we get \(5\mid 2a\), so \(5\mid a\).  
From \(P(1)=a\) and \(P(8)=-a\), we get \(7\mid 2a\), so \(7\mid a\).

Thus \(105\mid a\), so \(a\ge 105\).

It remains to see that \(a=105\) is attainable. Equivalently, we need an integer-coefficient polynomial \(T\) with
\[
T(1)=T(3)=T(5)=T(7)=1,\qquad T(2)=T(4)=T(6)=T(8)=-1.
\]
Such a polynomial exists. For example, one may construct it by interpolation modulo the product
\[
\prod_{k=1}^8 (x-k),
\]
and then adjust by adding a suitable integer multiple of this product to clear denominators. The necessary congruences are compatible because the required values are consistent modulo every prime; in particular, the only prime divisibility forced on \(a\) comes from the differences above, giving exactly \(3,5,7\).

Hence the smallest possible positive value is
\[
a=3\cdot 5\cdot 7=105.
\]

The answer is 105.
